chapters.title: Economy and investment climate
chapters.headline: Ghana's real GDP grew 6.0% in Q2 2026 (6.2% in H1) with inflation at 5.2% in September and the Bank of Ghana policy rate held at 14.0%, as the country exited its US$3bn IMF programme in July 2026.
chapters.summary: Ghana has moved from crisis recovery to post-programme consolidation: the IMF Board completed the final ECF review on 27 July 2026 and also reviewed a 36-month non-financing Policy Coordination Instrument (PCI) requested by the authorities. Growth remains solid (6.0% in Q2 2026, led by services and ICT at +30.9%), inflation is low at 5.2% (September 2026), public debt is 45.9% of GDP and gross reserves stood at US$12.0bn (4.5 months of imports) on 22 September 2026. The main macro watch-points are a cedi that has weakened 9.5% year-to-date to GHS 11.55/USD by 18 September 2026, a slower IMF growth projection of 4.9% for 2026, ratings still in single-B territory, and February 2027 domestic debt repayments. For investors, the new GIPA Act 2026 (Act 1173) removes blanket minimum capital for wholly foreign-owned firms and joint ventures, and press reports expect the 2027 Budget in the first week of November 2026.

rules.text: GIPA Act 2026 (Act 1173), assented 15 July 2026, converts GIPC into the Ghana Investment Promotion Authority, removes blanket minimum capital requirements for wholly foreign-owned enterprises and joint ventures, introduces a statutory Investor Grievance Mechanism, a One-Stop-Shop and annual registration renewal.

Section 31 of Act 1173 requires a non-citizen engaging in a trading enterprise to invest at least US$500,000 in cash equity, and at least 75% of all employees must be skilled Ghanaians. Section 32 lists six activities reserved for Ghanaians.

source2.label: Clyde & Co / Legal Ink – Understanding Ghana's new investment law (3 Sep 2026)

rules.text: Profit repatriation: Act 1173 protects the free transfer of capital, profits and dividends and retains protection against unlawful expropriation (law-firm summary; check the Act text before relying on specific clauses).

Free zones: a 10-year corporate income tax holiday (the rate after the holiday has changed over time; confirm it with GFZA and GRA); no withholding tax on dividends; duty-free imports for production; at least 70% of output must be exported (up to 30% may be sold locally); no restrictions on repatriation of dividends or net profit.

VAT reform under the VAT Act, 2025 (Act 1151), effective 1 January 2026: effective VAT rate 20% (15% VAT + 2.5% NHIL + 2.5% GETFund, with NHIL/GETFund now creditable as input tax), registration threshold for goods traders raised from GH₵200,000 to GH₵750,000, VAT Flat Rate Scheme and COVID-19 Health Recovery Levy abolished.

source2.label: Graphic Online – GRA announces VAT overhaul, COVID levy abolished from Jan 1 (30 Dec 2025)

rules.text: 24-Hour Economy incentives are still being designed: the Presidential Advisor said (Aug 2026) that packages will be performance-based (tied to jobs, investment and productivity), carry sunset clauses of typically four to five years, and that beneficiaries will be listed on a public register; details are due 'in the coming months'. Separately, existing investment law already lets investors above US$50m negotiate tailored incentive packages under specific conditions.

opportunities.text: Digital economy momentum: ICT led services growth in Q2 2026 at +30.9% y/y and contributed 41.5% of total GDP growth, while investment rose 53.0%, supporting demand for data, connectivity and software services.
Cheaper local credit: the average lending rate fell to 15.9% from 24.2% a year earlier, the 91-day T-bill to 5.4%, and private-sector credit growth rebounded to 35.5% in August 2026.

24-Hour Economy programme: the 24-Hour Economy Authority Act was assented in February 2026; announced incentives include 25% (two shifts) and 50% (three shifts) corporate tax rebates across eight sub-programmes (Grow24, Make24, Build24, Show24, Connect24, Fund24, Aspire24, Go24), though detailed incentive packages were still to be published as of August 2026.

Lower entry barriers under Act 1173: no general minimum capital for foreign-owned firms and JVs outside trading, plus a statutory grievance mechanism and GIPA 24-hour service for registrations, renewals and quota applications.

Public infrastructure pipeline: under the 'Big Push', 87 projects had commenced by mid-2026 and US$1.7bn was deposited in a dedicated account for the Accra–Kumasi expressway, creating supply-chain and contracting opportunities.

risks.text: Currency risk has returned: after strong appreciation in 2025, the cedi weakened 9.5% year-to-date to GHS 11.55/USD by 18 September 2026 (about GHS 11.76 by 6 October), and gross reserves fell from US$14.16bn (March 2026) to US$11.07bn (August 2026) before recovering to US$12.05bn on 22 September.
Growth expected to slow: the IMF projects real GDP growth of 4.9% for 2026, below the 6%+ prints of H1 2026; the government's 2026 budget target, unchanged at the mid-year review, is 4.8%.

source2.label: Citi Newsroom – 12 economic figures from the 2026 Mid-Year Budget Review (Jul 2026)

risks.text: Banking vulnerabilities persist in some state-owned banks, some private banks and specialised deposit-taking institutions (IMF).

Debt-service and refinancing: S&P kept Ghana at B-/B (Sept 2026), noting stronger reserves and exports have not removed constraints from high debt-service costs; the 2026 Mid-Year Budget Review targets a GHS30bn sinking fund by end-2026 to repay DDEP bonds falling due in February 2027.

source2.label: GNA – Highlights: 2026 Mid-Year Budget Review (23 Jul 2026)

risks.text: Export concentration and price inflation drift: gold accounted for US$14.86bn of US$22.44bn total exports (about 66%) in Jan–Aug 2026, and headline inflation has risen for two months, from 4.6% (July) to 5.0% (August) and 5.2% (September 2026).

source2.label: GBC – Inflation rises to 5.2% in September – GSS (7 Oct 2026)

chapters.title: Gold, mining and critical minerals
chapters.headline: Gold drives two-thirds of Ghana's exports as the state resets royalties, ASM trading and licensing rules
chapters.summary: Gold exports reached USD 14.86bn in January–August 2026 out of USD 22.44bn in total exports (Bank of Ghana), after a record USD 20.98bn in 2025. Output reached 5.94 million ounces in 2025 (up 23.4%, Ghana Chamber of Mines), with artisanal and small-scale mining (3.11 Moz) overtaking large-scale mines (2.83 Moz), and the Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod) is now the sole buyer and exporter of ASM gold. Since 10 March 2026 a sliding-scale gold royalty of 5% to 12% applies under L.I. 2517, partly offset by a cut in the Growth and Sustainability Levy from 3% to 1% of gross production. Ghana ratified its first lithium mining lease (Ewoyaa) in March 2026, and a draft Minerals and Mining Bill, 2026, which would replace the 2006 Act, shorten mining leases and give the state a special share, is awaiting Parliament, which makes regulatory change the main thing for investors to watch.

rules.text: Royalties: the Minerals and Mining (Royalties) Regulations, 2025 (L.I. 2517), in force since 10 March 2026, replace the flat 5% gold royalty with a price-linked scale. The rate is 5% up to US$1,900/oz and 6% from US$1,900 to US$2,000, then rises one point per US$500/oz band to 12% above US$4,500/oz. The gold price is the weekly average of the LBMA London PM price for the month's sales. Small-scale gold pays 2%, and lithium (spodumene) has its own 5%–12% scale. Diamonds, bauxite, manganese, iron ore and industrial minerals stay at 5%. At the Bank of Ghana's August 2026 average gold price of US$4,408.4/oz, the 11% band (above US$4,000 to US$4,500) would apply.
Growth and Sustainability Levy: in March 2026 Parliament passed an amendment cutting the levy on mining companies' gross production from 3% to 1%, to offset the new sliding-scale royalties.

Mineral rights (Minerals and Mining Act, 2006, Act 703) are granted by the Minister for Lands and Natural Resources on the recommendation of the Minerals Commission. The reconnaissance licence runs 12 months (up to 5,000 blocks of 21 ha). The prospecting licence runs 3 years (up to 750 blocks). The mining lease runs up to 30 years (up to 300 blocks) and the restricted mining lease up to 15 years for building and industrial minerals. The small-scale mining licence lasts 5 years and is reserved for Ghanaians only. The Government holds a 10% free carried interest in mining operations.

source2.label: Minerals Commission – Fiscal Regime (additional source for the 10% carried interest)

rules.text: Gold trading: under the Ghana Gold Board Act, 2025 (Act 1140), GoldBod has the exclusive right to buy, sell, assay, value and export ASM gold. Foreign nationals had to leave local gold trading by 30 April 2025, and dealing in gold without a GoldBod licence has been an offence since 1 May 2025. Licences held by large-scale mining companies were not revoked under this reset. From 1 September 2026, Self-Financing Aggregators must refine gold doré at a GoldBod-approved refinery in Ghana before export.

source2.label: Graphic Online, 15 Apr 2025 (GoldBod directive of 14 Apr 2025) – additional source

rules.text: Forest reserves: the Environmental Protection (Mining in Forest Reserves) Revocation Instrument, 2025 matured into law on 10 December 2025. It revokes L.I. 2462, which had allowed the President to authorise mining in forest reserves.

Local content and fiscal terms: the Minerals and Mining (Local Content and Local Participation) Regulations, 2020 (L.I. 2431) set local procurement, employment and participation requirements. Corporate income tax on mineral operations is 35%. Under current law, stability agreements can run up to 15 years, and development agreements are available for investments above US$500m.

opportunities.text: Large-scale exploration and mining rights are open to foreign-owned Ghanaian companies through the Minerals Commission's licensing process (reconnaissance, prospecting and mining lease), using the online mining cadastre. Small-scale licences remain reserved for Ghanaians.

Lithium: in March 2026 Parliament ratified Atlantic Lithium's Ewoyaa mining lease (announced 20 March 2026), the first lithium lease granted and ratified in Ghana (initial 15-year term, sliding royalty of 5% to 12%). The project is moving towards a final investment decision, creating openings for offtake, financing, EPC and services.
Refining and value addition: GoldBod's mandatory local refining of aggregator doré from 1 September 2026 creates demand for GoldBod-approved refining, assaying and logistics capacity in Ghana.

Bauxite and aluminium: GIADEC is seeking partners to build an integrated bauxite–alumina–aluminium value chain on an estimated 920 million tonnes of bauxite (Awaso, Nyinahin, Kyebi). It offers resource-for-credit swaps, long-term offtake and joint-venture partnerships (as at June 2025).

Mining services and supply chain: new large-scale capacity such as Newmont's Ahafo North (commercial production from October 2025, about 560 permanent and 1,000 contracted operating roles) needs contractors and suppliers. Foreign providers typically take part through partnerships that comply with the L.I. 2431 local content rules.

risks.text: Fiscal take: the L.I. 2517 royalty reaches 12% above US$4,500/oz. The Ghana Chamber of Mines warned that the increase would hit new projects immediately and put the projected 6.5 Moz output for 2026 at risk.

Legal reform: in July 2026 Cabinet approved a revised mining law for Parliament. A draft Minerals and Mining Bill, 2026 would replace the 2006 Act. It would replace reconnaissance and prospecting licences with a single exploration licence capped at five years, cut mining lease terms to 15 years (or the life of the mine, if shorter), give the state a special share, and require community development agreements negotiated with host communities. The government has also signalled plans to phase out fiscal stability agreements. The bill had not been debated as of end-September 2026 and could be taken up when Parliament resumes in October.

Lease renewal risk: the Damang mining lease was not renewed for Gold Fields beyond a one-year extension to 18 April 2026. After a tender, the Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources granted the lease to Engineers and Planners, which took over the mine on 18–19 April 2026. Gold Fields' main Tarkwa leases are due to expire in April 2027 (renewal applied for).

ESG and illegal mining (galamsey): the Forestry Commission recorded 8,923.8 ha of forest reserves degraded by illegal mining as at end-2024. In February 2026 the government announced a Ghana Armed Forces-led cleanup of water bodies and stronger NAIMOS enforcement. Investors face reputational, community and supply-chain due-diligence exposure.

Concentration and price exposure: gold makes up about two-thirds of export earnings and ASM supplies more than half of output. GoldBod based its 2026 forecasts on about US$5,000/oz, above recent prices, so export receipts and state gold purchases are sensitive to the gold price.

players.name: Minerals Commission
players.what: Main regulator for mineral rights. Receives and evaluates licence applications, runs the mining cadastre, inspects mines and makes recommendations to the Minister of Lands and Natural Resources.

players.name: Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod)
players.what: Set up under Act 1140 (2025) as the sole authority to buy, sell, assay, value and export ASM gold and other precious minerals. Licenses gold traders and aggregators and sets refining rules.

players.name: Newmont
players.what: Operates Ahafo South and Ahafo North (commercial production October 2025; 275,000–325,000 oz/yr guided over the next five years).

players.name: Gold Fields
players.what: Holds 90% of the Tarkwa mine, with the Government of Ghana holding 10%. Attributable Mineral Reserves are about 6.6 Moz (31 Dec 2025) and the CIL plant has 14.7 Mtpa capacity. The main Tarkwa leases expire in April 2027 (renewal applied for). Gold Fields exited Damang in April 2026.

players.name: AngloGold Ashanti
players.what: Owns 100% of the Obuasi underground mine (Ashanti Region; 266,000 oz in FY25) and also operates Iduapriem.

players.name: Zijin Mining
players.what: Completed its US$1bn acquisition of the Akyem open-pit gold mine from Newmont on 16 April 2025.

players.name: Asante Gold
players.what: Listed on TSXV and GSE; operates the Bibiani and Chirano gold mines. 2026 guidance is 275,000–300,000 oz at an AISC of US$3,200–3,600/oz.

players.name: Atlantic Lithium
players.what: Developer of the Ewoyaa lithium project (Central Region), holder of Ghana's first ratified lithium mining lease (ratified March 2026).

chapters.title: Oil and gas, power and renewables
chapters.headline: Jubilee drilling reverses a six-year oil decline while power-sector finances improve but remain the main investor risk
chapters.summary: Ghana's crude output fell for a sixth consecutive year in 2025 to 37.3 million barrels, but a 2026 Jubilee infill campaign lifted oil and gas activity by 22.4% in Q2 2026, and oil exports reached US$2.42bn in January–August 2026. Jubilee and TEN licences have been extended to 2040, which brings up to 20 additional Jubilee wells; a further 10-well campaign is signed for 2027–28. The power system has 5,818 MW installed and depends on thermal plants for about three-quarters of generation. The IMF reports the energy-sector shortfall fell to US$1.4bn in 2025, but legacy payables to IPPs and fuel suppliers were still US$1.7bn in March 2026, so offtaker credit risk remains the central issue for power investors.

rules.text: Local content (L.I. 2204, 2013): an indigenous Ghanaian company other than GNPC must hold at least 5% equity for a party to qualify for a petroleum agreement or licence; a foreign company supplying goods or services to the upstream sector must form a joint venture giving an indigenous Ghanaian company at least 10% equity. Operators must also run bidding processes that give preference to indigenous companies.

Renewable Energy Act, 2011 (Act 832), s.8: any commercial activity in the renewable energy industry needs an Energy Commission licence. This covers production, transport, storage, distribution, sale, import, export and installation/maintenance.

Act 832 as amended by Act 1045 (2020), s.25: renewable electricity bought by public utilities and wholesale suppliers must go through a competitive procurement scheme (tender or auction). Public utilities may not negotiate PPAs for renewable power unless it has gone through an open, competitive and transparent procurement process.

Net metering (Act 832 s.30A, inserted 2020): a statutory net-metering scheme for renewable self-generation. Under s.26, distribution utilities must procure renewable electricity from consumer-generators.

PURC resets electricity and water tariffs every quarter. It indexes them to the cedi–dollar rate, inflation, the weighted average cost of gas (US$7.8379/MMBtu used for Q4 2026, down from US$7.9708 in Q3) and the hydro–thermal generation mix. For Q4 2026 (1 Oct–31 Dec) the change is 0%.

Energy Commission standards and labelling regulations (in force since November 2022; enforced from November 2023 after a one-year transition) cover solar panels (L.I. 2449), renewable-energy batteries (L.I. 2452) and inverters (L.I. 2461). Importers must register products with the Energy Commission (accredited test reports) and meet labelling requirements.

opportunities.text: Upstream services and drilling supply chain. Tullow's 2025–26 Jubilee campaign was completed in September 2026, with six producers and one water injector onstream. A rig contract for a 2027–28 campaign of up to 10 wells is signed, with the rig expected around mid-2027. The Jubilee and TEN licence extensions to 2040 (ratified February 2026) allow up to 20 additional Jubilee wells. Service firms must meet the 10% indigenous joint-venture rule.

Gas supply and processing. GRIDCo's 2025 Electricity Supply Plan put firm Jubilee/TEN/OCTP supply at about 416 mmscf/d. It also identified a need for additional gas volumes to meet thermal demand. Eni says OCTP meets about 70% of gas demand for power generation, and Eban-Akoma (declared commercial July 2025) is set to become a new source of supply.

Utility-scale solar plus storage for industry. Up to 1.5 GW of solar with battery storage is being developed at Buipe under the government's 24-Hour Economy (24H+) Programme. The joint development agreement was signed on 10 April 2026, and in July 2026 the presidential adviser said construction of the first 100 MW would begin in August 2026. The target is to cut industrial power costs from 18–23 to 7–9 US cents/kWh.

Commercial and industrial (C&I) and rooftop solar under net metering. Grid supply is about 74% thermal, and the law provides a net-metering scheme and a renewable purchase obligation on distribution utilities. Together these support behind-the-meter solar for factories, mines and commercial property.

Distribution private-sector participation. The IMF reports that a transaction adviser has been appointed to procure ECG concessionaires, with concessions expected to be awarded by June 2027. This is an entry point for distribution operators, metering and loss-reduction contractors.

risks.text: Offtaker payment risk. Net payables to IPPs and fuel suppliers were still US$1.7bn at end-March 2026. The IMF projects a sector shortfall of about US$1.1bn in 2026, driven by collection and distribution losses, and warns the sector is prone to slippages during electoral periods.

Mature-field production decline. Ghana's crude output fell for the sixth consecutive year in 2025, down 22.7% to 37.3m barrels. New Jubilee wells lifted output in 2026 (about 72,000 bopd gross in Q2; GNPC cites more than 80,000 bopd in September), but sustaining it depends on continued infill drilling in mature fields.

Fiscal and tax disputes. On 30 September 2026 an ICC tribunal found that a US$196.5m corporate income tax assessment on Tullow was not in breach of its petroleum agreements. Investors should model the risk of tax claims under stability clauses.

Currency and tariff risk. Revenue is in cedis while gas and many IPP contracts are priced in dollars. PURC tariffs move quarterly with FX and gas costs (Q2 2026: -4.81%; Q3: +3.49%; Q4: 0%), so cedi depreciation or a tariff freeze compresses cost recovery.

Thermal and gas dependence. Thermal plants supplied 74.33% of generation in July 2026, and PURC's Q4 2026 tariff assumed a mix that is 75.75% thermal (79.10% in Q3). Supply depends on domestic gas availability and pricing, which exposes generators and offtakers to field outages and gas cost changes.

chapters.title: Cocoa, agribusiness and agro-processing
chapters.headline: Cocoa earnings rise and financing is moving onshore, as a 50% local-processing mandate begins with the 2026/27 season
chapters.summary: Bank of Ghana data show cocoa exports of USD 2.76bn for January–August 2026, up from USD 2.47bn a year earlier, although gold still accounts for most export earnings. COCOBOD has replaced its decades-old offshore syndicated loan with a GH¢16.3bn domestic notes programme run by its subsidiary Cocoa Capital PLC, and opened the 2026/27 season at GH¢42,400 per tonne (about 27% below the 2025/26 opening price) (71.18% of realised gross FOB, above the 70% floor in the new Ghana Cocoa Board Act, 2026). From 2026/27, Cabinet policy requires at least half of the cocoa crop to be processed locally, while the 13 existing grinders run at only 30–40% of about 500,000 tonnes of installed capacity. Beyond cocoa, the investment case rests on import substitution (2025 food imports were GH¢36.46bn), cashew and shea processing, and cold chain. Swollen shoot disease, illegal mining, smuggling, EUDR compliance from 30 December 2026 and cedi volatility are the main risks.

rules.text: The Ghana Cocoa Board Act, 2026 (Act 1182) requires farmers to receive at least 70% of the realised gross FOB price. Haulier, buying-margin, warehousing and inspection rates for 2026/27 are unchanged.
In February 2026 Cabinet approved a directive requiring at least 50% of Ghana's cocoa beans to be processed locally, starting with the 2026/27 crop season.

Non-citizens (including companies with more than 40% non-citizen ownership) may hold land only as leasehold, for no more than 50 years at any one time (Land Act 2020, Act 1036, s.10). Any grant of freehold to a non-citizen is void. A fixed-term lease to a non-Ghanaian is not renewable unless the lease expressly provides for renewal (s.50(17)), so renewal terms must be negotiated up front. Registered leases can be mortgaged.

Free zone enterprises pay no income tax for 10 years (confirm the rate that applies afterwards with GFZA and GRA, as it has changed). Imports for production are duty-free and dividends are exempt from withholding tax. At least 70% of output must be exported, so up to 30% may be sold locally.

Outside free zones, agro-processors that mainly use local raw materials get a 5-year concessionary period. GRA calls it a tax holiday, but its table shows a 5% special rate during it. After that, location-based rates apply: 5% in the Northern, Upper East and Upper West Regions, 10% outside regional capitals, 15% in other regional capitals and 20% in Accra/Tema. Tree-crop farming gets a 10-year concessionary period, and exporters of non-traditional products pay a concessionary 8% rate. GRA's guidance is internally inconsistent, so confirm current rates with GRA.

The Ghana Investment Promotion Authority Act, 2026 (Act 1173, assented 15 July 2026) replaces Act 865. It removes blanket minimum capital requirements for wholly foreign-owned enterprises and joint ventures, keeping thresholds only for trading. It also adds a one-stop shop and an investor grievance mechanism.

opportunities.text: Cocoa grinding and semi-finished products. The 13 local processors run at only 30–40% of about 500,000 t of installed capacity, and the 50% local-processing mandate from 2026/27 is meant to direct more beans to local grinders. This creates openings for capacity revival, working-capital finance and offtake.

Domestic cocoa paper. Cocoa Capital PLC's GH¢16.3bn programme (GH¢14bn of commercial paper for 2026/27 purchases, GH¢2.3bn of bonds to refinance legacy debt) is repaid from assigned forward-sales receivables through ring-fenced accounts. The Finance Minister said the paper would be issued in three tranches over an 8-month season and would widen participation to pension funds and non-resident investors. The first 266-day tranche raised GH¢3.39bn against a GH¢4bn target at 11% (October 2026).

source2.label: Adom Online, 5 Oct 2026 (first CP tranche result)

opportunities.text: Import substitution in rice and poultry. GSS puts the 2025 food import bill at GH¢36.46bn. The Feed Ghana coordinator reports rice sufficiency up from 42% to 56% and poultry from 5% to 21%, which still leaves a large gap for integrated poultry, feed and rice-milling investment.

Cashew and shea processing. A Nitidae/ACPG study found Ghana processed only about 15,000 t of raw cashew in 2025, under 6% of estimated output of 262,000 t, while about 444,000 t of raw nuts (including informal imports from neighbours) were exported. In July 2025 the government announced a phased ban on raw shea-nut exports from 2026. GEPA reports shea-nut exports more than doubled to USD 177.79m in 2025, partly because exporters front-loaded shipments ahead of the ban.

Cold chain and processed food for AfCFTA markets. The US International Trade Administration (2022) put the revenue potential of cold-chain solutions in Ghana's fruit and vegetable value chains at up to USD 900m a year. Government is repositioning special economic zones around agro-processing and offering rules-of-origin support for AfCFTA trade, with the AfCFTA Secretariat based in Accra.

risks.text: Cocoa swollen shoot virus disease. In February 2024 COCOBOD's then chief executive said more than 500,000 hectares of cocoa farms had been lost to it. This constrains bean supply for processors and the long-term outlook for output.

Illegal mining (galamsey) on farmland. A 2022 COCOBOD study reported more than 19,000 ha of surveyed cocoa farms destroyed or affected (some outlets reported acres). The damage was concentrated in the Eastern, Western and Ashanti regions, which produce over 90% of the crop. This covers selected farms, not a national total, and COCOBOD said in 2024 it had no up-to-date national data.

Smuggling. A COCOBOD official estimated losses of almost USD 1.1bn to cocoa smuggling into Togo and Côte d'Ivoire over 2022–2025. Recorded output in Volta/Oti collapsed from 7,215 t (2020/21) to 87 t (2024/25).
EU Deforestation Regulation compliance. EUDR applies to cocoa exports from 30 December 2026, so traceability and geolocation gaps could disrupt shipments to the EU.

FX and financing. The cedi depreciated 7.1% against the USD in the year to end-August 2026, and 9.5% by 18 September 2026 (BoG). Crop finance now depends on domestic money-market appetite for COCOBOD paper rather than offshore syndicated loans.

chapters.title: ICT and fintech, manufacturing, real estate and logistics
chapters.headline: ICT leads Ghana's growth and mobile money exceeds GH¢500bn a month, while ports run near capacity and industrial policy has moved from 1D1F to the 24-Hour Economy (24H+) framework
chapters.summary: Ghana's Statistical Service reported ICT growth of 30.9% year-on-year in Q2 2026, the main driver of 6.0% real GDP growth, and Bank of Ghana data show monthly mobile money transactions of GH¢518.8bn in August 2026. The new Ghana Investment Promotion Authority Act, 2026 (Act 1173) removes blanket minimum capital for non-trading foreign enterprises, and the 24-Hour Economy Authority Act (assented February 2026) is the new channel for manufacturing incentives after the One District One Factory programme was discontinued in 2025. Housing remains structurally short (deficit estimated at over 1.8 million units), with non-citizens limited to leaseholds of up to 50 years, renewable only if the lease says so. Container traffic through Tema and Takoradi rose 12.2% in January–May 2026, but congestion at Tema and slow delivery of inland port and rail projects are binding constraints.

rules.text: Act 1173 repeals Act 865 and removes the general minimum-capital rule for foreign-owned non-trading enterprises and joint ventures. Section 31 sets US$500,000 cash equity for a non-citizen trading enterprise and requires at least 75% of all employees to be skilled Ghanaians. Section 49 sets expatriate-quota bands of 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 or 12 positions for directly invested capital from US$50,000 to above US$10 million; a registered enterprise applies in writing and the Authority decides on Immigration Service advice. A quota is distinct from a work permit. Foreign-owned registrations renew annually; wholly Ghanaian-owned enterprises may register voluntarily and renew if registered.

Bank of Ghana licenses non-bank payments under seven categories: Dedicated Electronic Money Issuer, PSP Scheme, PSP-Enhanced, PSP-Medium, PSP-Standard (reserved for Ghanaians and wholly Ghanaian-owned entities), Payment and Financial Technology Service Provider, and Digital Credit Services Provider. Applications go through the BoG FinTech & Innovation Office; a regulatory sandbox admitted six firms for one year in January 2026 to test virtual-asset products.
Data Protection Act, 2012 (Act 843): all data controllers and processors must register with the Data Protection Commission.

Free Zones Act, 1995 (Act 504): free-zone enterprises must export at least 70% of annual output (up to 30% may be sold locally) and may be 100% foreign-owned. GFZA lists a 10-year corporate income tax holiday, exemption from duties on imports for production, and exemption from dividend withholding tax. EY (Oct 2025) reports that the reduced post-holiday rate and dividend exemptions were repealed by later tax laws, so confirm the post-holiday rate and dividend treatment with GFZA and GRA before modelling.

Land Act, 2020 (Act 1036), s.10(6), and Article 266 of the Constitution: no leasehold exceeding 50 years at any one time may be granted to a non-citizen. The lease is renewable; freehold is not available to non-citizens.

Real Estate Agency Act, 2020 (Act 1047): anyone who, for a fee, lists, markets, sells, buys, rents or leases property on behalf of others must be licensed by the Real Estate Agency Council as a real estate broker or agent. The Council keeps a transaction database and works with the Financial Intelligence Centre on anti-money-laundering compliance.

24-Hour Economy Authority Act (assented 19 Feb 2026) creates the authority that coordinates 24H+ incentives. The published 24H+ package (Aug 2025) includes import-tax exemptions on manufacturing machinery and some inputs, CIT reductions for two- and three-shift operations, priority power and water access for three-shift operators, and a local value-addition rebate (G-LVAR). President Mahama has proposed duty- and tax-free import of expansion and retooling equipment for factories registered under the initiative. Confirm which measures have been enacted in tax law.
The Electronic Transfer Levy (E-Levy, 1%) on mobile money and electronic transfers was abolished by the Electronic Transfer Levy Repeal Bill 2025, approved by Parliament on 26 March 2025.

opportunities.text: Payments and embedded finance: mobile money reached GH¢518.8bn and 1.05bn transactions in August 2026, but only about 26.4m of 85.8m registered accounts are active. This leaves room for merchant acquiring, cross-border remittance and B2B payments (PSP-Enhanced licence), digital credit (Digital Credit Services Provider licence or bank partnership) and KYC, scoring and fraud tooling (PFTSP licence).

Fixed broadband and data infrastructure: mobile data penetration is 87.65%, but fibre broadband had only 273,095 subscriptions and Starlink 28,612 in Q1 2026. This points to underbuilt fixed, enterprise-connectivity and hosting capacity behind 30.9% ICT growth.

Tech talent and offshore delivery: the government's One Million Coders Programme, rolled out nationally in April 2026, targets 300,000 trainees in 2026 across 130 learning centres. It is a pipeline for software, AI and cybersecurity operations.

Export manufacturing and agro-processing: multi-shift plants can combine 24H+ CIT reductions, duty-free equipment and the G-LVAR rebate. Free-zone status (100% foreign ownership, 10-year tax holiday) and lower GIPA entry thresholds suit export-oriented, AfCFTA-facing production; 50 states had ratified AfCFTA by October 2025.

Housing and building materials: a deficit officially estimated at over 1.8 million units, urbanisation above 50% and stalled affordable-housing schemes create demand for mid-market housing delivery, rental platforms, construction finance and local materials. Non-citizens are limited to 50-year renewable leases.

Port-centric logistics: container traffic is growing at double digits and Tema is congested, while the US$308m Boankra inland terminal is behind schedule and seeking funding. Opportunities include off-dock container yards, bonded warehousing, inland logistics and transit corridors to Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger.

risks.text: Port congestion: in September 2026 the Transport Minister ordered urgent action at Tema after container volumes 'increased almost to 100 per cent' and system outages at the MPS terminal. Expect demurrage, delays and off-dock diversion during peak season.

Infrastructure delivery: Boankra inland terminal construction achieved only 6% against a 20% milestone for April 2026, and phase one, due in Q1 2025, is still unfinished. The Tema–Mpakadan railway needed a US$21m EU grant (July 2026) to fix signalling and other systems that were incomplete at commissioning. Do not base logistics plans on rail or inland-port capacity yet.

Industrial policy discontinuity: the Trade Minister told Parliament on 8 July 2025 that 'there is no policy as 1D1F' and that no incentives currently applied under it, with the ministry still assessing the fallout for 1D1F companies. Incentives under the successor 24H+ programme depend on the new Authority and enabling tax measures.

Free-zone tax erosion: EY (Oct 2025) reports that Act 504's reduced post-holiday rate (8%) and dividend exemptions were repealed, with domestic sales taxed at the standard 25% CIT; the same note cites 15% on export profits after the holiday. GFZA still advertises a maximum of 8%. Confirm the applicable rate with GRA before modelling.

Telecom market concentration: MTN Ghana holds 80.10% of mobile data subscriptions and 72.5% of mobile voice subscriptions (June 2026). Pricing, interconnection and significant-market-power rules can change quickly for entrants and partners.

source2.label: National Communications Authority, Monthly Industry Voice June 2026

risks.text: Regulatory and ownership limits in fintech and land: PSP-Standard licences are reserved for Ghanaians; all data controllers must register with the DPC; non-citizens cannot hold land leases above 50 years at a time. Title diligence through the Lands Commission is essential.

outlook.title: Outlook 2026–2028
outlook.lead: Our view of where Ghana’s economy is heading, in three scenarios. Each starts from the official forecasts of the IMF, the World Bank, the Bank of Ghana and the Ministry of Finance, and adds our reading of the drivers that matter most: gold, cocoa, oil, the cedi and public finances.

scenarios.name: Base case
scenarios.story: Growth stays around 5% as the gold boom cools but ICT, services and oil keep expanding. Inflation drifts back into the Bank of Ghana’s 8% ± 2 band as the cedi weakens gradually, so rate cuts are slow. The February 2027 domestic bond repayments are met from the sinking fund.
assumptions: Gold about US$4,700/oz in 2026 and US$4,300 in 2027 (World Bank, April 2026)
Cocoa about US$3.80/kg in 2026 and US$4.20 in 2027 (World Bank, April 2026); our assumption of a smaller 2026/27 crop
Oil output above 100,000 barrels a day in 2026 (our assumption; Jubilee alone above 80,000 b/d per GNPC), rising further as new Jubilee wells come on stream
Primary surplus of 1.5% of GDP in 2026 (legislated floor) and 0.5% from 2027 (proposed in the 2026 Mid-Year Review; requires amending the PFM Act)

scenarios.name: Upside
scenarios.story: Gold stays above US$4,500 into 2027, new Jubilee wells push the field above 90,000 barrels a day and the cocoa crop recovers. Reserves rise towards six months of imports, the cedi is broadly stable and the Bank of Ghana can cut rates further.
assumptions: Jubilee above 90,000 barrels a day from 2027
Fiscal discipline holds through the 2028 election year

scenarios.name: Downside
scenarios.story: Gold falls back towards US$3,800, the cocoa crop disappoints and election-cycle spending returns. With large domestic bond repayments in 2027–2028, the cedi weakens faster, inflation moves above the target band and the Bank of Ghana has to raise rates again.
assumptions: Cocoa crop near or below 650,000 tonnes
Fiscal slippage ahead of the 2028 general election

indicators.label: Real GDP growth
indicators.why: H1 2026 grew 6.2%; we expect a slower second half as the oil boost fades. Official forecasts (4.8% for 2026) look cautious; Fitch Solutions expects 5.7%.

anchors.quote: Real GDP growth is projected at 4.8 percent in 2026
GDP growth is projected to moderate to 4.8 percent in 2026
Fitch Solutions forecasts Ghana's economy to grow by 5.7% in 2026

indicators.label: Inflation, end of year
indicators.why: Inflation (5.2% in September) is below the 8% ± 2 target band. The Bank of Ghana expects it to move up into the band over the next few quarters as higher utility tariffs and fuel prices pass through; Fitch Solutions expects a weaker cedi to push it to 9% by end-2026.

anchors.what: IMF: 8.0% at end of each year
anchors.quote: return within the BoG target band (8±2 percent) by end-2026
the medium-term target range of 8 ± 2 percent

indicators.label: Bank of Ghana policy rate, end of year
indicators.why: With inflation near 5% the real policy rate is about 9%, very high; but rising inflation and a weaker cedi argue for holding in November and cutting slowly.

anchors.quote: voted by a unanimous decision to maintain the Monetary Policy Rate at 14.0 percent

indicators.label: Cedi per US dollar, end of year
indicators.why: The cedi has lost 9.5% this year after a 40.7% gain in 2025. Our base case assumes about 10% a year of depreciation from 2027, more in the 2028 election year.

anchors.quote: stronger foreign exchange inflows and an improving external position
the cedi traded at GH¢11.55 to one American greenback

indicators.label: Gross reserves, months of imports
indicators.why: Reserves fell from US$14.2bn in March to US$11.1bn in August; a lower gold price would slow the rebuild the IMF expects.

anchors.what: IMF: 4.5 / 5.0 / 5.5 months of prospective imports (IMF basis; not comparable with BoG import cover)

sectors.base: Margins stay strong even with the sliding royalty; watch the Minerals and Mining Act amendments on stability agreements.
sectors.up: Record export earnings; strongest case for new large-scale projects and local refining.
sectors.down: A lower gold price and the higher royalty bands squeeze new projects; small-scale output falls first.

sectors.base: New Jubilee wells support output; power offtaker arrears remain the key risk for IPPs.
sectors.up: Output back above 100,000 barrels a day; more room to clear energy arrears.
sectors.down: Arrears build up again; prefer commercial and industrial solar with private offtakers.

sectors.base: Lower world cocoa prices cut export earnings; the 50% local-processing mandate supports grinders.
sectors.up: Crop recovery plus processing incentives make 2027 a good entry point for processors.
sectors.down: A small crop and EU deforestation rules hit volumes; traceability becomes a must-have.

sectors.base: Still the fastest-growing sector; a weaker cedi raises the cost of imported equipment.
sectors.up: Strong demand for payments, data centres and software services.
sectors.down: Growth slows but stays positive; cedi revenue loses value in dollars.

sectors.base: High interest rates keep mortgages scarce; demand for mid-market housing remains.
sectors.up: Rate cuts open up mortgage finance and construction activity.
sectors.down: Higher rates and a weaker cedi raise building costs and stall projects.

sectors.base: A gradually weaker cedi favours exporters with costs in cedis.
sectors.up: A stable cedi helps importers and companies with dollar debt.
sectors.down: Dollar earners win; importers and dollar borrowers should hedge.

outlook.method: Scenarios start from the latest official projections and add our judgement on the drivers listed. They are estimates from public data, not a statistical model, and not investment advice. We review them every quarter and after major data releases, and keep a public scorecard of our forecasts against the outcomes.
